description: Solo team working on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. I'm building a quick-comparison tool for lunar south pole landing sites that evaluates solar power and direct-to-Earth communication using real LOLA terrain and JPL ephemerides, validated against NASA illumination maps.
summary: At the lunar south pole the Sun and Earth hug the horizon, so a hill one degree high can decide between power and darkness, or between talking to Earth and silence. Our web app lets mission planners, educators and the public compare landing sites and dates in seconds. It computes Sun and Earth positions with JPL ephemerides, builds each site's true horizon from NASA LOLA terrain, and shows sunlight, Earth visibility, time to sunset and Earthset, solar power and battery needs. NASA's Artemis III candidate regions serve as a reference set of real south pole sites, alongside past landings and any custom coordinates; each mission sets its own required surface stay. A landing calendar shows which site works on each day of the year, and a 100 m view shows how small landing errors change the outcome. Results are validated against JPL Horizons, NASA's LOLA illumination maps and real missions including Chandrayaan-3 and Apollo 11.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

A web app for comparing lunar south pole landing sites and dates in seconds. For any two sites it shows where the Sun and Earth sit above the real local horizon, how long each stays up, and what that means for solar power, batteries and direct-to-Earth communication.

- Landing calendar: for every day of a year, which candidate site gives continuous sunlight for the mission's surface stay (user-set; 6.5 days for Artemis III by default), shaded by Earth visibility.

- Side-by-side comparison: sunlight, solar elevation, Earth in view, longest darkness and communication blackout, landing windows.

- Time slider: Sun and Earth elevation, clearance above terrain, and hours until sunset or Earthset at any moment.

- Sky view, 360° horizon panorama with an animation, and 3D terrain with cast shadows and NASA's long-term sunlight and Earth-visibility maps.

- Power and battery: output of a vertical Sun-tracking panel and the battery needed for a constant load, sized by energy balance.

- 100 m landing-error view, matching the accuracy of precision landers.

- Sites: NASA's Artemis III candidate regions as a reference set, past landings (IM-1, IM-2, Chandrayaan-3, Apollo 11), or custom coordinates.

- Terrain on/off switch to show what a smooth-sphere calculation gets wrong.

HOW IT WORKS

Sun and Earth positions come from Skyfield with the JPL DE421 ephemeris and the Moon's mean-Earth frame, including libration and no atmospheric refraction. Each site's horizon is the highest terrain angle in 360 directions out to 150 km, from LOLA elevation models with lunar curvature correction. A body counts as visible when any part of its disc clears that horizon, the same rule NASA uses for its illumination maps. Heavy terrain work is precomputed so the app responds in seconds.

WHAT WE FOUND

- No single site works year-round. For the 6.5-day Artemis III stay in 2027, each candidate region works on 124 to 278 days; together they leave only 19 days without an option.

- On ridges, 100 m decides Earth contact. At Malapert Massif, 100 m north keeps Earth in view all the time, 100 m south roughly halves it. NASA's own map shows the same boundary.

- Terrain cuts both ways: crater floors stay dark, while high ridges see below the flat horizon and gain Sun and Earth time.

- A few hours of grazing sunlight can split a long darkness on paper but barely recharge a battery. Energy-balance sizing catches this.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

When a launch slips or a site changes, planners can re-check alternative sites and dates in seconds instead of running separate tools. Educators and the public can see, in one picture, why the lunar south pole is so hard: the Sun circling the horizon, Earth rising and setting with libration, and terrain deciding both.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- A landing calendar that turns a year of ephemeris and terrain data into one image of which site works on which day.

- A 100 m sensitivity view that shows how landing error alone can change communication time.

- A power model that sizes batteries by energy balance rather than counting hours of darkness.

- Checks against real missions: predicted sunset at Chandrayaan-3 matches when ISRO put the lander to sleep, and Sun and Earth elevations at the Apollo 11 landing match the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy: positions checked against the JPL Horizons API at six sites for every day of 2027 (largest difference 0.000013°); 18.6-year sunlight within 4 percentage points of NASA's LOLA illumination maps; IM-1 terrain height 2,592 m vs 2,579 m from LROC.

- Honesty about limits: 80 m terrain near each site (a 20 m check changes horizons by 0.01–0.12° at most sites but up to 2° on the Malapert ridge), coarser terrain for custom coordinates with an on-screen warning when results are position-sensitive, and an ideal panel model.

- Speed: precomputed horizons and local ephemerides so every interaction responds in seconds without depending on an external service.

- Accessibility: a plain-language explainer, tabs for different questions, and colour conventions kept consistent (amber for the Sun, blue for Earth).

TOOLS

Python, Streamlit, Plotly, Skyfield, NumPy, pandas; rasterio, pyproj and SciPy for offline terrain processing. Deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud. Full method, validation and limitations: README and docs/validation.md in the repository.
